clinician.trajectory_summary: A 22-month-old boy presented with a 3-week history of fever, cough, and night sweats, accompanied by severe respiratory compromise (oxygen saturation 89% on room air, dyspnea, chest indrawing, tachypnea, right-sided crackles). Physical examination revealed wasting (weight 8.4 kg, weight-for-height Z score <-3), fever (39.8°C), tachycardia, and pallor. Initial chest radiograph showed heterogeneous opacification in the right lower lobe, middle lobe, and right upper lobe. Laboratory investigations revealed elevated TLC of 103,000 cells/µl with left shift (neutrophils 84.2%, bands, metamyelocytes), microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 5.08 g/dl), and markedly elevated CRP of 102.5 mg/l—findings consistent with acute bacterial infection rather than leukaemia. Blood cultures were negative. The patient was treated with intravenous antibiotics (ampicillin and gentamicin) and tuberculosis medications. Clinical improvement occurred within 3 days of antibiotic initiation, with resolution of fever, respiratory distress, and cough, and progressive weight gain. The patient was discharged after 17 days of hospitalization with normalized TLC (7,670 cells/µl). The diagnosis of necrotizing pneumonia is supported by the clinical presentation of severe pneumonia with systemic toxicity, the imaging findings of heterogeneous opacification in multiple lobes, the marked inflammatory response (elevated TLC with left shift and high CRP), and the rapid clinical response to antibiotics.
